The lemma claims finite transversals = those containing one of finitely many B_j. Is this true for pairwise intersecting infinite families? Consider F = {{2}∪g : g∈G} ∪ {{1,2}}. Wait, the family must be pairwise intersecting. The witness: C={c1,c2}, F={C}∪{{c2}∪g: g∈G}. Is F pairwise intersecting? {c2}∪g intersects C in c2; two members {c2}∪g, {c2}∪g' intersect in c2. Yes, pairwise intersecting regardless of G. Transversals: X must meet C, so contain c1 or c2; and must meet each {c2}∪g. If c2∈X, done. If X avoids c2, must contain c1 and be a transversal of G. Choose G with infinitely many minimal transversals, e.g. G = sets {n, n+1} for n≥... wait minimal transversals: G = {{n, n'} : n∈ℕ} pairs (2k-1,2k): minimal transversals are choosing one from each pair — infinitely many incomparable. Then finite transversals avoiding c2 include {c1, choice of one from each pair} — infinitely many pairwise incomparable minimal transversals. So no finite list. The lemma is false as stated.

Hmm, but the induction proof: where does it fail? The induction: "for each c∈C, by induction hypothesis there is a finite list D_{c,k}". But F_c need not be pairwise intersecting? F_c = {F: c∉F}. Members of F_c all contain c2 (in witness for c=c1... wait). In the witness, with C from F: lemma's proof chooses C∈F, so C = {c1,c2} (as a member). F_{c1} = sets not containing c1 = {{c2}∪g : g∈G}. Is F_{c1} pairwise intersecting? Members {c2}∪g, {c2}∪g' intersect in c2 — yes. And transversals of F_{c1} include c2 alone... wait {c2} is a transversal of F_{c1}. So C\{c1} = {c2} is a transversal. Induction on |C|=1: F_{c1} pairwise intersecting with transversal {c2}. Then F_{c2} within that = sets not containing c2 = empty. So transversals of F_{c1}: those containing c2 OR (c1's case). Hmm, actually the criterion: X traverses F iff {c}∪D_{c,k} ⊆ X for some c∈X∩C and k. For X = {c1}∪t where t is transversal of G: X∩C = {c1}, need {c1}∪D_{c1,k} ⊆ X for some k, i.e. D_{c1,k} ⊆ t. D_{c1,k} comes from transversals of F_{c1}... but the recursion: D_{c1,k} are from the list for F_{c1}, whose transversals are X meeting every {c2}∪g. If X contains c2 fine, but X avoiding c2 needs transversal of G. Recursion on F_{c1} with C={c2}: c2's subfamily is empty family, D_{c2,1}=∅, giving {c2} as pattern. But that only covers transversals containing c2 — transversals of F_{c1} avoiding c2 need transversals of G, which the induction doesn't capture because induction only handles transversals meeting C! Indeed the proof says "we only need to restrict attention to transversals meeting C" — that's the flaw: the induction statement restricted to transversals meeting C fails to propagate, because F_c's transversals restricted to meeting C\{c} doesn't cover all. Actually the proof asserts transversals meeting C suffice "because C∈F" at top level — true there — but the inductive step: X traverses F, X meets C. Criterion: contains c∈X∩C and D_{c1,k}. But D_{c1,k} describes transversals of F_{c1} meeting C\{c1}? No — the induction hypothesis gives list for transversals of F_{c1} meeting C\{c1} = {c2}. A transversal X of F avoiding... containing c1 but not c2: X∩(C\{c1}) may be empty, so X's status as transversal of F_{c1} is not captured by lists describing only transversals meeting {c2}. The witness's G shows genuinely infinitely many incomparable patterns. So the lemma is false; witness correct.
